chunks: What was narrated by Ali ibn Ja'far from his brother Musa ibn Ja'far (peace be upon him) — he said:
I asked him about a mouse that fell into a jar of oil and was removed before it died — can we sell it to a Muslim?
He said: Yes, and you may anoint yourself with it, and this does not contradict what...

key_terms.تَدَّهِنُ: you may anoint yourself — Form VIII verb (ادّهن), meaning to apply oil to the body; indicates permissible personal use
key_terms.حُبِّ دُهْنٍ: jar of oil — a large earthenware vessel (حُبّ) used to store oil or fat; not 'love' (the more familiar sense of حُبّ)
key_terms.فَأْرَةٍ: mouse/rat — the animal whose contact with the oil raises the ritual purity question
key_terms.يُنَافِي: it contradicts/is incompatible — Form III of نافى; Tusi's editorial term for apparent conflict between narrations

ai.seo_question: In Shia Islamic law, if a mouse falls into a jar of oil but is removed alive before dying, is the oil still pure and permissible to sell and use?
ai.summary: Ali ibn Ja'far poses a practical jurisprudential question to Imam Musa al-Kazim (AS): if a mouse falls into a large jar of oil but is extracted alive, does the oil retain its purity and remain permissible? The Imam's ruling is affirmative on both counts — it is lawful to sell the oil to a Muslim and to use it for personal anointing. The condition of the mouse being removed alive (قَبْلَ أَنْ تَمُوتَ) is the pivotal legal factor, distinguishing this case from the stricter ruling applied when the animal dies in the oil. The truncated closing phrase (وَلَا يُنَافِي ذَلِكَ مَا) is the editorial formula Shaykh al-Tusi uses in al-Istibsar to introduce reconciliation with apparently contradictory narrations.
